clue.text: Brand accepts plan backing guarantee

indicators.note: the brand word takes the reversed plan inside it

parts.note: a make is a brand of product, as in 'what make is your car?'

indicators.note: backing means going backwards, so the word is reversed

parts.note: a ruse is a cunning plan

explanation.surface: A company signs up to a plan that comes with a guarantee.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backing' turns RUSE into ESUR, and 'accepts' puts that inside MAKE, after MAK.
explanation.definitionFit: To make sure is to ensure or confirm, the verb sense of guaranteeing an outcome.

clue.text: Start to watch broadband supplier's strand

indicators.note: 'Start to' points at the beginning of the action named next, so only the opening letter of that word is wanted.

parts.note: the first letter of watch
an internet service provider is the firm that sells you broadband

explanation.surface: A viewer tunes in to a broadband provider whose service hangs by a thread.
explanation.walkthrough: ISP is worth banking: setters reach for it whenever broadband, the web or a connection turns up, and three of the four letters arrive in one go.
explanation.definitionFit: strand → WISP: a wisp is a single thin strand of hair, smoke or straw — one trailing piece rather than a bundle.

clue.text: Subsection of secret summons turned around rally

indicators.note: A subsection is a piece cut out of something longer, which is the instruction: take a run of letters from inside the words that follow.
Turned around means facing the other way, so that run of letters has to be read from its far end back.

parts.note: secRET SUMmons carries RETSUM, which reads the other way as the answer

explanation.surface: Part of a confidential order has gone astray, and a rally is called.
explanation.walkthrough: A hidden run almost always straddles a word boundary, because your eye reads whole words and skips the join — and here it is buried backwards as well.
explanation.definitionFit: rally → MUSTER: to rally troops is to muster them, both verbs meaning to gather scattered people into one body ready for action.

clue.text: One who keeps quiet before the Guardian's outcry

indicators.note: 'Before' is positional, not temporal: the piece it follows is laid down first and the next one comes after it.

parts.note: someone who clams up gives nothing away
the paper printing this puzzle calls what belongs to it ours

explanation.surface: A tight-lipped informant comes ahead of a newspaper row.
explanation.walkthrough: A paper naming itself in its own crossword is a Guardian regular — read the italicised title as the word the paper would use for its own property.
explanation.definitionFit: outcry → CLAMOUR: a clamour is the loud protesting din a crowd raises, which is exactly the public complaint an outcry names.

clue.text: A female or male tennis icon?

parts.note: the article is taken as it stands
'female' is a common stand-in for the three-letter subject pronoun

explanation.surface: A quiz question asks whether a famous tennis star was a woman or a man.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is the sex change: two words for a woman spell a man. Arthur Ashe won Wimbledon in 1975 and has New York's main court named after him.
explanation.definitionFit: male tennis icon → ASHE: definition by example, naming one particular great of the game rather than giving a synonym for a player.

clue.text: Chamber's diet for those chosen

definitions.meaning: the debating chamber where a country's laws are argued
a diet is a formal assembly — Japan still calls its own one — and its members are the elected

explanation.surface: The legislature serves up what its elected members are fed.
explanation.walkthrough: The trap is 'diet' as food. In politics a diet is an assembly, so both halves of the clue are describing the same institution from different angles.
explanation.definitionFit: Both halves name the assembly: it is the chamber a nation debates in, and it is the diet — the sitting body — made up of those the voters chose.

clue.text: Late meeting of party in bishop's office

indicators.note: 'In' is doing spatial work rather than joining a phrase: what precedes it goes inside what follows.

parts.note: a bishop's office and district is his see
the African National Congress, South Africa's governing party

explanation.surface: A party gathers late in the evening at the bishop's residence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Late' is the obituary sense — the late Mr Jones — so this is a meeting with the dead, not one that runs past six o'clock.
explanation.definitionFit: Late meeting → SEANCE: a sitting at which a medium tries to contact the dead, so the gathering really is with those who have died.

clue.text: It's normal for holiday at Legoland at the outset to involve a little something for everyone

indicators.note: involving means taking in, so the initials are wrapped around the other pieces
the outset is the start, so the opening letter of each of these words is taken

parts.note: first letters of holiday, at and Legoland
a bit is a little
U, universal, is the British film certificate for a film suitable for all ages

explanation.surface: A theme-park holiday is said to be standard fare, with a bit of fun for the whole family.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at the outset' gives HAL; 'to involve' puts A + BIT + U inside it after H. U is the British film rating meaning suitable for everyone.
explanation.definitionFit: Habitual means usual or customary, done by habit, so it describes what is normal for someone.

clue.text: See 10
Spooner's expensive rendezvous with The Blob?

definitions.note: a nickname for an unseen, amorphous network of officials, hence the question mark

indicators.note: Rev. Spooner famously swapped the opening sounds of words, so the starts of the two words change places

parts.note: steep means expensive, as in steep prices
a date is a rendezvous

explanation.surface: Someone pays dearly for a date with the monster from the 1958 horror film The Blob.
explanation.walkthrough: Swapping the opening ST and D of STEEP DATE gives the answer. 'The Blob' is a disparaging British nickname for the civil service establishment.
explanation.definitionFit: The deep state is the supposed hidden network of officials steering policy, which critics in Britain call the Blob.

clue.text: I tremble in feverish place where the fuel runs out?

definitions.text: place where the fuel runs out?

indicators.note: a feverish person is agitated and restless, so these letters are shaken into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone shivers with fever, wondering where the petrol ran out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'feverish' looks like part of the trembling but signals rearranging I TREMBLE IN. The fuel is wood: above this line no trees grow.
explanation.definitionFit: The timberline is the altitude above which trees cannot grow, so the supply of wood for burning ends there.

clue.text: Relish killing

definitions.meaning: the slang sense of falling on something with great appetite, as in a familiar phrase about craving a curry
the crime itself, one person unlawfully killing another

explanation.surface: Someone takes ghoulish delight in a killing.
explanation.walkthrough: Two words, two senses, and a nastier surface than either deserves. It is also one of this grid's collective nouns — crows come in one.
explanation.definitionFit: The plain sense is the crime, killing someone unlawfully; the slang sense is the appetite of 'I could murder a pint', devouring something with relish.

clue.text: Thwart fickle rule in gear shift?

parts.note: to derail a plan is to thwart it

indicators.note: something fickle keeps changing, so these letters change their order

explanation.surface: Someone foils a changeable regulation about changing gear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fickle' rearranges RULE to LEUR, placed after DERAIL.
explanation.definitionFit: A derailleur is the bicycle mechanism that moves the chain between sprockets, shifting gears.

clue.text: Open to the elements, caps missing, air processor burned

indicators.note: caps are tops, the first letters; with missing, it tells each of the two words to lose its opening letter

parts.note: a lung is the organ that processes the air we breathe

indicators.note: missing completes caps missing, which applies to both words: the second word too lacks its top letter

parts.note: blazed means burned fiercely

explanation.surface: A machine handling air has its covers off and burns out in the open.
explanation.walkthrough: 'caps missing' works on both words together: LUNG loses its L to give UNG, and BLAZED loses its B to give LAZED.
explanation.definitionFit: Unglazed means without glass, so a window frame left so is exposed to wind and rain.

clue.text: Sport cut short leg

indicators.note: cutting short removes the end, so the word loses its last letter

parts.note: a game is a sport

explanation.surface: A sporting fixture is curtailed by a leg injury.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leg' sounds like a stage of a game, but it is the body part, from slang.
explanation.definitionFit: Gam is old American slang for a leg, especially a woman's shapely leg.

clue.text: Unravel slam point

parts.note: to slam a film in a review is to decry it
PT is the standard abbreviation for point, as on a chart

explanation.surface: A critic's savage review makes its point plain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slam' invites you to think of doors and dunks; the wanted sense is the reviewer's. With no indicator anywhere, the two pieces simply sit end to end.
explanation.definitionFit: Unravel → DECRYPT: to decrypt a message is to unravel it, turning a scrambled cipher back into sense the way you unpick a knot.

clue.text: Hope to God every third letter appears in books made to order

definitions.note: The definition names what comes off the press rather than the process: POD is print on demand, a way of making books, and the clue defines it by its output.

indicators.note: This is a counting instruction rather than a description: walk through the preceding words in threes and keep only the one you land on.

parts.note: HOPETOGOD falls into HOP, ETO, GOD, and the third letter of each group is what is kept

explanation.surface: An author prays that a book printed on request will appear.
explanation.walkthrough: Print on demand is the publishing trade's own abbreviation: a title is printed only once somebody has bought a copy, so no stock sits in a warehouse.
explanation.definitionFit: books made to order → POD: print on demand, the trade's term for running off a copy only after it has been ordered.

clue.text: Mammoth setter's crew stripped user

parts.note: the setter refers to themself as I, and setter's means setter is, I'M
the crew are the men

indicators.note: stripped of its outer layers, the word keeps only its middle letters

parts.note: middle letters of user

explanation.surface: The setter's team undresses a drug user, a hulking figure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'setter's' is setter is, I'M; 'stripped' takes the ends off USER, leaving SE.
explanation.definitionFit: Mammoth as an adjective means enormous, the same as huge or vast.

clue.text: Smartening up University College in April and May

indicators.note: in means the abbreviations sit inside the season

parts.note: April and May are spring months

explanation.surface: Students tidying up a university college during the spring term.
explanation.definitionFit: Sprucing means making neat and tidy, as in sprucing oneself up.

clue.text: Offensive in the armed forces?

definitions.note: The second definition is a phrase where the answer is an adjective: the setter is reading 'civil' as civilian, so somebody serving in the forces is literally un-civil.
definitions.meaning: the everyday sense — rude, discourteous, giving offence
a soldier is not a civilian and not in the civil service, so not civil

explanation.surface: Soldiers mount an attack, or perhaps just behave rudely.
explanation.walkthrough: Everything hangs on which 'civil' you hear: polite in one half, civilian in the other. The question mark is the setter owning up to the second one.
explanation.definitionFit: Offensive → UNCIVIL means rude or discourteous; the forces half plays on the other sense of civil, the one that means civilian rather than polite.

clue.text: Walked free in road house

definitions.note: 'Walked' serves as both past tense and past participle, and only the participle sense matches: you have walked, you have stridden.

indicators.note: 'In' says the piece before it drops inside, landing between the two short words that follow.

parts.note: street shortens to ST on any address
a den is a small private room in a house
to be free of something is to be rid of it

explanation.surface: A prisoner strolls out of a roadside inn.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'roadhouse' as one word, which is the trap — road and house are clued separately, and the participle is one solvers forget exists.
explanation.definitionFit: Walked → STRIDDEN: the past participle of stride, which is walking with long purposeful steps, so it fills the same slot after 'has'.

clue.text: Some leaderless after god proving hard to please

indicators.note: 'After' fixes the order against the surface: the piece named first ends up behind the one named second.

parts.note: Thor, the Norse god of thunder
some is any, which loses the A at its head

explanation.surface: A few followers left without a leader turn to a deity and prove difficult.
explanation.walkthrough: Norse gods are crossword furniture — THOR, ODIN, LOKI all fit tight spaces. Here the god's name is laid down first even though the clue mentions him second.
explanation.definitionFit: hard to please → THORNY: a thorny character is prickly to deal with, snagging on whatever is offered, so nothing you bring them is ever right.

clue.text: Sew up ruptured uterus

indicators.note: A ruptured thing has burst apart, and once the letters are in pieces they can be put back in any order.

parts.note: the six letters of UTERUS, rearranged

explanation.surface: A surgeon stitches up a torn womb.
explanation.walkthrough: Surgical from end to end: what ruptures is the very thing you stitch, so fodder and definition belong to one scene rather than fighting each other.
explanation.definitionFit: Sew up → SUTURE: the surgeon's verb for stitching a wound closed, the technical word sitting under the everyday phrase.

clue.text: Ask Einstein to include networks

indicators.note: To include is to contain already, so the letters are sitting inside the words as written rather than being built.

parts.note: aSK EINStein runs the letters straight through the gap between the words

explanation.surface: Someone asks the great physicist to bring computer networks into his work.
explanation.walkthrough: A famous name is where setters like to bury things: you read Einstein as a person and never as six letters carried over from the word before.
explanation.definitionFit: networks → SKEINS: a skein is a loose coil of yarn, and the word carries over to any tangle of interwoven lines or connections.

clue.text: Ten solutions may provide tonic with novel clues

indicators.note: the letters may provide something new when rearranged, a loose signal to reorder them

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Ten crossword answers come with a tonic of fresh clues.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' looks like the usual signal to rearrange, but here its letters are part of the mix with TONIC and CLUES. Ten grid answers, such as MURDER, PACK, POD and PARLIAMENT, are group terms for animals.
explanation.definitionFit: A collective noun names a group, such as a murder of crows; ten answers in this grid are such words.

clue.text: Whack the top guy and stay mum

parts.note: the commanding officer is the man in charge of a unit
SH is the noise you make telling someone to keep quiet

explanation.surface: A thug knocks out the boss and keeps quiet about it.
explanation.walkthrough: CO for commanding officer is worth banking: it turns up whenever a clue mentions a boss, an officer or whoever is in charge.
explanation.definitionFit: Whack → COSH: to cosh somebody is to hit them with a heavy stick or bar, so it is one particular kind of whack.

clue.text: Begging your permission, tread carefully

definitions.note: 'Pace' is the Latin preposition English borrowed — pace Dr Johnson — meaning 'with all respect to', which is why a whole polite phrase defines one short word.
definitions.meaning: the bookish word used before disagreeing with someone, by their leave
the plain English verb for walking in measured, deliberate steps

explanation.surface: Someone politely asks leave before advising caution.
explanation.walkthrough: Two different words share one spelling — one straight out of Latin, one plain English — which is how the clue defines it twice without repeating itself.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin pace begs leave before contradicting someone; the English verb means to step out a distance deliberately, one measured stride at a time.

clue.text: Wild Bunch get ready to hit the road

definitions.meaning: wolves and hounds run in one

definitions.text: get ready to hit the road
definitions.meaning: filling a case is what you do before a journey

explanation.surface: A gang of outlaws prepares to ride out of town.
explanation.walkthrough: The capitals point at the western film, which is the misdirection; the wolves' word is also one of the collective nouns this grid keeps turning up.
explanation.definitionFit: A wild bunch is what a pack of wolves running loose amounts to, and to pack is to fill your bags before setting off on a trip.

clue.text: See 24
Local, having no cash, in the clear

parts.note: your local is the pub, an inn
O is the round nothing, as written on a scoresheet
a cent is the smallest coin of American cash

explanation.surface: A penniless pub regular is cleared of all charges.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the back half as a sum of money — nought cents, not a bean — and the penniless regular of the surface stops getting in the way.
explanation.definitionFit: in the clear → INNOCENT: somebody cleared of a charge is innocent of it, the courtroom verdict and the everyday phrase meaning the same thing.
